messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Vignette:
Thomas is a 69-year-old widowed financial analyst who came to treatment after several years of trying to keep his life narrowed to work, routine, and anything that did not touch grief. The event he returns to, often without warning, is his wife’s death. He describes the day in clear fragments rather than as a story he can tell straight through. He remembers being in the hospital room, the mechanical sounds around her bed, the pause before staff moved in, and the moment he understood that the effort to save her had stopped. What remains with him most sharply is not a broad account but a set of abrupt impressions: the stillness in her face, the unnatural quiet after the activity in the room, and the realization that he was leaving the hospital alone. Even now, a memory of that moment can come to mind suddenly, cutting into whatever he is doing before he has any chance to prepare.

In the months after her death, Thomas did what he has always done when overwhelmed: he made himself functional. He returned to his job, sat through meetings, reviewed spreadsheets, and spoke in the measured tone people expected from him. Colleagues described him as steady. From his side, it felt less like steadiness than shutting everything down. He numbed his feelings because allowing any of them in seemed dangerous; he was certain that if he really let himself feel the loss, he would lose control in a way he could not recover from. He tried hard not to think about the hospital room, the funeral, or the fact of being a husband one day and a widower the next. When thoughts came anyway, he pushed them away and turned back to numbers, market reports, and deadlines.

Over time, his world became organized around not being reminded. He avoids anything that pulls him toward grief. If coworkers begin talking about someone who has lost a spouse or parent, Thomas finds a reason to step out or abruptly changes the subject. What unsettles him is not only sadness but the immediate sense that the room has become dangerous, as if a door has opened onto the same moment he has been trying to outrun. At work, where retirement planning and estate discussions sometimes overlap with clients’ recent losses, he has become noticeably terse. He has cut meetings short and snapped at younger colleagues when they linger on a bereavement story or use sentimental language about family. He knows the sharpness in his voice is more than the situation requires, but in those moments he feels flooded with anger, fear, and something like guilt, all at once, and his body reacts before he can compose himself. He describes his chest tightening, his stomach dropping, and a rush of heat through his arms when grief-related topics come up unexpectedly.

Funerals and cemeteries have become especially potent. He attended his wife’s funeral in a state he recalls as almost anesthetized, focused on logistics and handshakes rather than the service itself. Since then, he has refused invitations to memorials and will not visit her grave. He tells himself there is no point in going, but in session it becomes clearer that what frightens him most is the prospect of standing there and being hit again by the same finality he felt that day. Even driving past a cemetery is enough to change his breathing and put him on edge for hours. If he sees mourners gathered outside a church or hears of a neighbor’s burial, the hospital memory can arrive with such force that for a moment he feels jerked backward in time.

This way of living has cost him. As a widower, Thomas has already had to tolerate a quieter home than he ever wanted; his efforts to keep grief out have made that quiet more absolute. Friends have stopped asking him to join them for memorial services or anniversaries because he always declines or becomes visibly uncomfortable. At work, where he once had a reputation for patience, he has become irritable enough that others now approach him carefully when conversations might involve death or family loss. He dislikes this version of himself and feels ashamed after angry outbursts, yet he also feels justified in the moment, certain that if people would stop bringing these things up, he could hold himself together.

He sought help only recently after a conversation in the office about a colleague’s widower father left him trembling in the restroom, furious at himself and unable to regain his concentration for the rest of the day. He was struck by how quickly the memory had overtaken him and by how small his life had become around avoiding reminders. Thomas says he does not expect to “get over” his wife’s death. What he hopes, more modestly, is to be able to hear ordinary talk about loss, pass a cemetery, or sit with a memory of her without feeling as though he is back in that hospital room, and without becoming someone he no longer recognizes.
